fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of Pre-Hospital Tourniquet in Emergency Patients with Major Trauma and Uncontrolled Haemorrhage: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract Trauma is one of the leading causes of uncontrolled haemorrhage, death, and disability. Use of a tourniquet can be considered an optimal anti-haemorrhagic resource, in pre-hospital and emergency settings, and its lifesaving effect is clinically contradictory. This review aims to assess the clinical efficacy of the tourniquet in the emergency pre-hospital care setting for the management of haemorrhage. We conducted the systematic review following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, the PRISMA statement. We searched the following electronic databases: EMBASE, MEDLINE, and Cochrane-CENTRAL. All studies included were appraised for risk of bias. Prevalent primary outcomes were mortality and use of blood products. Secondary outcomes were related to adverse effects. The quality of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach (GRADE). Four studies were involved (1762 trauma patients). The adjusted odds ratio (aOR) of 0.47 (95% confidence Interval (CI) 0.19–1.16; three studies; 377 patients) for overall mortality estimates did not give a clear indication of the benefits of emergency pre-hospital tourniquets (PH-TQ) versus no pre-hospital tourniquet (NO PH-TQ) placement. The adjusted mean difference for blood product use was −3.28 (95% CI −11.22, 4.66) for packed red blood cells (pRBC) and −4.80 (95% CI −5.61, −3.99) for plasma, respectively. The certainty of evidence was downgraded to very low for all outcomes. Our results suggest an unclear effect of emergency pre-hospital tourniquet placement on overall mortality and blood product use. However, this systematic review highlights the availability of only observational studies and the absence of high quality RCTs assessing the efficacy of PH-TQs. Randomized controlled trials are needed. Keywords: systematic review, tourniquet, haemorrhage, emergencies, meta-analysis 1. Introduction Every year, the lives of about 1.35 million people are cut short as a result of trauma caused by road traffic crashes, and between 20 and 50 million people worldwide suffer non-fatal injuries [1], with many incurring a disability [2]. Uncontrolled bleeding is the leading cause of death in 34% of trauma patients. Haemorrhage is one of the major causes of potentially preventable deaths in both civilian and military contexts [3]. The Italian National Institute for Statistics recorded a total of 172,183 traumas in 2019 [4], which, according to the Multi-Regional Serious Trauma Intra-Hospital Centre [5], was prevalent in the male population (75.7%), and 65.4% (n = 4385) required intensive care unit (ICU) hospitalization with a mean stay of 7.3 days (standard deviation = ±14.6), a fatal outcome of 27.5%, and 17.4% of patients requiring transfusions in the emergency room [6]. Bleeding control in major trauma is a clinical priority that can be achieved through either direct compression or the use of mechanical or pneumatic tourniquets (TQ). Direct pressure is the first and simplest step. TQs can be applied if direct pressure on the bleeding area is not sufficient to control the bleeding [7] and when direct pressure is not a feasible option. Direct pressure should be maintained by health care personnel, which is sometimes insufficient in number. Use of a TQ can be considered an optimal anti-haemorrhagic resource in an emergency setting, and its lifesaving effect has become more apparent [8]. The use and effectiveness of mechanical or pneumatic TQs appears to be associated with effective control of bleeding and lower mortality rates from bleeding [9]. This is why the Hartford Consensus Conference [10] encourages their widespread use among the civilian population for the early control of haemorrhage in the extremities (upper and lower limbs) when direct manual compression is ineffective or unfeasible. In the literature, the efficacy of TQ application for the management of bleeding in the pre-hospital phase in patients with major trauma is supported by relatively low, often contradictory evidence, or is even not recommended for use in the civilian context [8]. In particular, it remains an open question whether when used in the pre-hospital setting, it leads to better survival and a reduced need for blood, or blood component, transfusions. This systematic review aims to summarize current knowledge on the clinical efficacy of pre-hospital TQ, which has been used as a framework to support the development of Italian guidelines for pre-hospital emergency treatment of major trauma (MT) in civilian settings. 2. Materials and Methods We conducted a systematic review to support the major trauma integrated management guideline panel of the Italian National Institute of Health (NIH) in formulating recommendations [11]. Following the GRADE-ADOPOLMENT methodology [12], and in accordance with the standards defined by the NIH [13], the multidisciplinary panel decided to apply a structured and systematic updating and adaptation process of their recommendations from the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) guideline NG39 on pre-hospital application of TQs [14]. We conducted the systematic review following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, the PRISMA statement [15]. Study protocol has been stored at the following link: https://osf.io/n526s/ (accessed date 29 November 2021). fetched_contents.text: Prehospital Tourniquets in Civilians: A Systematic Review Abstract Objectives: Terrorist attacks and civilian mass-casualty events are frequent, and some countries have implemented tourniquet use for uncontrollable extremity bleeding in civilian settings. The aim of this study was to summarize current knowledge on the use of prehospital tourniquets to assess whether their use increases the survival rate in civilian patients with life-threatening hemorrhages from the extremities. Design: Systematic literature review in Medline (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Cochrane Library, and Epistemonikos was performed using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Guidelines. The search was performed in January 2019. Setting: All types of studies that examined use of tourniquets in a prehospital setting published after January 1, 2000 were included. Primary/Secondary Outcomes: The primary outcome was mortality with and without tourniquet, while adverse effects of tourniquet use were secondary outcomes. Results: Among 3,460 screened records, 55 studies were identified as relevant. The studies were highly heterogeneous with low quality of evidence. Most studies reported increased survival in the tourniquet group, but few had relevant comparators, and the survival benefit was difficult to estimate. Most studies reported a reduced need for blood transfusion, with few and mainly transient adverse effects from tourniquet use. Conclusion: Despite relatively low evidence, the studies consistently suggested that the use of commercial tourniquets in a civilian setting to control life-threatening extremity hemorrhage seemed to be associated with improved survival, reduced need for blood transfusion, and few and transient adverse effects. Keywords: first responder, hemorrhage, penetrating wounds, tourniquet Introduction Trauma in the civilian setting may differ from trauma in the military, but the last decades’ terrorist attacks and mass-casualty events world-wide have made penetrating injuries more similar in the two settings than before. Therefore, knowledge from both settings can be valuable when informing national guidelines. This new panorama of injuries, often with multiple casualties occurring at the same time, has forced a re-evaluation of treatment and first responder recommendations. In the US, early hemorrhage control has become a central focus for improving survival in life-threatening extremity bleeding following the Hartford Consensus.1–4 They recommend that civilian bystanders, law enforcement officers, and Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel be equipped with and use tourniquets. In the last few years, Europe has had numerous terrorist attacks and mass-casualty events, including Oslo/Utøya 2011, Paris 2015, Nice 2016, and Berlin 2016. After the July 22, 2011 attacks in Norway,5 the Norwegian Directorate of Health (Oslo, Norway) published a report in which one of the recommendations was to establish updated national guidelines for the use of tourniquets by police officers. Few countries have coherent national guidelines for the use of tourniquets. Some systematic reviews already exist on the subject, but few had sufficiently broad search strategy, were published in English, and included both military and civilian studies. A new systematic review was therefore considered necessary. This systematic review aims to summarize current knowledge of the use of prehospital tourniquets to be used as a theoretical framework for developing guidelines for prehospital treatment in civilian settings. The primary outcome was to assess whether the use of prehospital tourniquets increases the survival rate in civilian patients with life-threatening hemorrhage from the extremities. Secondary outcomes were number of transfusions, complications, and other adverse events, if available. Methods To conduct this systematic review, the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) Guidelines6 were utilized (checklist is included in Appendix I; available online only). The protocol was published on PROSPERO (ID-number: CRD42019123172). Differences between Protocol and Review As described in the Introduction, penetrating injuries in civilian settings are more similar to such injuries in military settings now than they were before. Studies in military settings were therefore included. It was suspected that there would be few controlled studies on this intervention, and all types of study designs were identified. However, only studies with more than 20 cases were included in the primary outcome (mortality). All studies were included when assessing the secondary outcomes (blood transfusions, complications of the extremity, or other adverse events) to identify rare complications. These decisions were made before the search was done and before the inclusion process. Inclusion Criteria To identify all relevant studies on the topic, the following inclusion criteria were used: (1) Population: Adult patients aged ≥16 with life-threatening hemorrhages from the extremities; (2) Intervention: Treatment with tourniquet by professionals or laymen; (3) Comparison: Hemorrhage control with other measures; (4) Outcomes: Mortality, number of blood transfusions, complications of the extremity, and other adverse events - studies had to report on patient outcomes; (5) Study Design: All studies with more than 20 informants for primary outcome and all studies for secondary outcomes; (6) Language: All languages that could be translated by automatic translation engines were included, however, Cyrillic and Chinese papers were excluded; and (7) Publication Year: Studies published from 2000 onwards. Submission received: 26 November 2024 / Revised: 2 January 2025 / Accepted: 6 January 2025 / Published: 9 January 2025 Abstract Background and Objectives: Trauma, particularly uncontrolled bleeding, is a major cause of death. Recent evidence-based guidelines recommend the use of a tourniquet when life-threating limb bleeding cannot be controlled with direct pressure. Prehospital hemorrhage management, according to the XABCDE protocol, emphasizes the critical role of tourniquets in controlling massive bleeding. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to summarize data from the available scientific literature on the effectiveness of prehospital tourniquet use for extremity bleeding. Materials and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was performed between March 2022 and March 2024, adhering to PRISMA guidelines, to determine whether prehospital tourniquets are clinically effective. The analysis showed a non-statistically significant reduction in mortality risk with tourniquet application (4.02% vs. 6.43%, RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46–1.07). Clarify how different tourniquet types are defined and reported in trauma literature

The available evidence suggests that trauma literature often distinguishes pre-hospital tourniquet use from other tourniquet use or other bleeding control measures, but the definitions are not uniformly standardized across studies. In general, pre-hospital tourniquet use refers to tourniquet application by lay responders, first responders, or emergency medical services (EMS) at the scene or during transport, whereas “other” tourniquet use may be interpreted as tourniquet placement in the trauma center or later in the hospital setting [N3-R2][N5-F4]. The cited evidence also indicates that tourniquets are sometimes contrasted with direct pressure, hemostatic dressings, or other bleeding control techniques in the same injury context [N1-F3].

In the included search results, tourniquet classification in trauma literature is often tied to the timing and setting of application rather than a strict anatomical or device-type distinction. One source explicitly defines “pre-hospital tourniquet” as a measure used to control bleeding after severe traumatic bleeding, and limb tourniquet application is mentioned as a specific technique [N3-R2]. Another source emphasizes that civilian prehospital tourniquets are used by professionals or laymen to control life-threatening extremity hemorrhage, while the broader review notes that some studies include military and civilian settings and compare tourniquets with other measures [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This implies that the literature often frames pre-hospital tourniquet use as a category of early, scene-based bleeding control, while “other tourniquet use” can be interpreted more broadly, including hospital-based tourniquet placement or other contemporaneous interventions [N5-F4].

The evidence also shows that classification can affect outcome interpretation. For example, one study distinguishes between patients who received tourniquets before trauma center arrival (T-PH) versus after arrival (T-TC) and finds that delayed tourniquet use was associated with worse physiology and higher mortality from hemorrhagic shock [N5-F4]. Another source reports that civilian prehospital tourniquet use was associated with improved survival, but the review explicitly notes that most studies were highly heterogeneous and had low-quality evidence, which suggests that how tourniquet use is classified may influence conclusions about survival benefit [N2-R1][N2-R2]. A meta-analysis on pre-hospital tourniquets similarly notes that the evidence base is observational and that outcomes were adjusted for key confounders, reinforcing the importance of careful classification for meaningful comparison [N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence indicates that pre-hospital versus other tourniquet use is usually defined by setting and timing, not by tourniquet type alone [N3-R2][N5-F4]. However, because studies differ in how they operationalize “other tourniquet use” and whether they control for indication, mechanism, and injury severity, classification can substantially affect outcome interpretation [N1-F1][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N8:
Assess methodologic quality and limitations of the available studies

The available evidence points to several methodologic strengths and weaknesses in the studies cited here. A major strength is that many of the included studies are observational cohort studies or systematic reviews/meta-analyses, which are the best available design for evaluating real-world tourniquet use in trauma when randomized trials are lacking [N1-F1][N1-F2]. These studies often attempt to adjust for key confounders and report mortality and transfusion outcomes, which is important for estimating causal effects in observational data [N1-F1][N1-F2]. One meta-analysis explicitly included cohort studies with adjusted results for injury severity, age, depth of shock, and degree of head injury, and it used GRADE to assess evidence quality [N1-F1].

A major limitation is that the evidence base is predominantly observational, which introduces confounding and bias risks. The same meta-analysis notes that all included studies were observational and that the certainty of evidence was downgraded to very low for all outcomes [N1-F1]. Another review similarly states that the evidence was low quality and highly heterogeneous, with most studies reporting increased survival in the tourniquet group but few having relevant comparators, making it difficult to estimate survival benefit directly [N2-R1][N2-R2]. This heterogeneity suggests that studies may differ in population, injury severity, setting, and outcome ascertainment, which reduces comparability [N2-R1].

Indication bias is another important limitation. Several studies separate patients by indication status, which is methodologically useful, but it can also reflect selection bias if the indication itself is related to injury severity or prognosis. For example, one study found that patients with indication for tourniquet placement were more likely to survive when tourniquets were applied early, but the same study also reported that delayed tourniquet use was associated with worse physiology and higher mortality from hemorrhagic shock [N5-F4]. This suggests that the observed benefit may partly reflect selection of more severe or more indicated patients rather than a pure treatment effect. A second source similarly notes that civilian prehospital tourniquet use was associated with improved survival, but the review acknowledges that most studies had low-quality evidence and that the survival benefit was difficult to estimate [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Selection bias is also present because the studies are often retrospective cohorts or non-randomized observational designs. One meta-analysis of pre-hospital tourniquet studies found that PH-TQ use did not appear to significantly influence mortality, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.19–1.16) and very low-certainty evidence [N1-F1]. Another source reports a non-statistically significant reduction in mortality risk with tourniquet application (4.02% vs. 6.43%, RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46–1.07), again with low certainty [N1-F3]. These results highlight the instability of observational estimates and the need for caution in interpreting effect sizes.

Outcome measurement and adjustment are mixed. Some studies report mortality as the primary outcome and use multivariable adjustment, which is a strength [N4-R4][N5-F4]. Others report outcomes such as transfusion requirements, amputation, or adverse effects, but the evidence base is weaker for those outcomes [N1-F1][N1-F3]. The meta-analysis notes that outcomes were adjusted for key confounders, which is important, but it also notes that the evidence was very low quality [N1-F1]. The review on civilian prehospital tourniquets similarly states that the studies were heterogeneous and had low-quality evidence, with most reporting increased survival but few with relevant comparators [N2-R1][N2-R2].

In summary, the methodologic quality of the available evidence is limited by observational design, heterogeneity, low certainty, and potential confounding. Studies are strongest when they adjust for injury severity, mechanism, and other key covariates, but their results should still be interpreted cautiously because indication bias, selection bias, and limited adjustment can distort the observed associations [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N7:
Summarize the existing evidence on mortality outcomes by tourniquet use type

The evidence base for mortality outcomes by tourniquet use type is mixed and primarily observational. Several studies and meta-analyses directly or indirectly compare pre-hospital tourniquet application with other tourniquet use or no tourniquet use, but the results are not consistently supportive of a strong mortality benefit [N1-F1][N1-F3][N2-R1][N5-F4].

A key meta-analysis of pre-hospital tourniquet studies reported that use of pre-hospital tourniquet (PH-TQ) did not appear to significantly influence mortality; the adjusted odds ratio was 0.47 (95% CI 0.19–1.16), and the evidence was downgraded to very low certainty [N1-F1]. Another meta-analysis of limb hemorrhage found a non-statistically significant reduction in mortality risk with tourniquet application (4.02% vs. 6.43%, RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46–1.07), with no significant reduction in mortality or blood product use [N1-F3]. This suggests that, across observational studies, the mortality benefit is small and not statistically robust.

A civilian prehospital tourniquet review reported that most studies were highly heterogeneous with low-quality evidence and that most studies reported increased survival in the tourniquet group, but few had relevant comparators, making it difficult to estimate survival benefit directly [N2-R1][N2-R2]. A study comparing civilian prehospital tourniquet use with non-tourniquet use reported mortality of 5.2% in the non-tourniquet group versus 3.9% in the tourniquet group, but the association was not statistically significant (odds ratio 1.36; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.65; p = 0.452) [N4-R4]. This illustrates that some studies find a lower mortality rate in the tourniquet group, but the evidence remains weak and inconsistent.

A major limitation is that many studies are retrospective cohort studies, and the evidence is therefore subject to confounding and bias. One study of civilian trauma patients found that late trauma-center tourniquet use was associated with worse physiology and higher mortality from hemorrhagic shock, with delayed tourniquet use showing 4.5-fold increased odds of death compared to pre-hospital tourniquet use [N5-F4]. This study clearly separates pre-hospital tourniquet use from delayed hospital-based use and provides one of the strongest direct comparisons in the evidence base. It also shows that outcomes differ by setting: pre-hospital tourniquet use was associated with better survival than delayed tourniquet placement [N5-F4].

The evidence also indicates that outcomes may differ by trauma mechanism and injury severity. The trauma-center tourniquet study found that 70% of patients had blunt mechanism of injury, and it controlled for year of admission, mechanism of injury, and shock upon arrival [N5-F4]. Another source notes that civilian prehospital tourniquet use was associated with improved survival, but the review explicitly states that the evidence was low quality and highly heterogeneous [N2-R1][N2-R2]. This implies that the mortality benefit may vary by setting and injury context, but the literature is too inconsistent to draw a clear, robust conclusion.

Overall, the existing evidence does not support a strong, consistent mortality benefit of pre-hospital tourniquet application over other tourniquet use or no tourniquet use. The reported mortality rates are generally low, but the confidence intervals are wide, and the results are not statistically significant in many studies [N1-F1][N1-F3][N4-R4]. The most direct comparison in the evidence base is the trauma-center tourniquet study, which found that delaying tourniquet use to the trauma center was associated with worse outcomes [N5-F4]. However, because the studies are observational and heterogeneous, the conclusions should be interpreted cautiously [N2-R1][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N10:
Compare tourniquet use vs no tourniquet across trauma settings and outcomes

The available evidence suggests that tourniquet use is generally associated with lower mortality compared to no tourniquet use, but the effect is not consistently statistically significant across studies and is highly dependent on setting and injury context. The strongest direct evidence comes from a civilian trauma-center tourniquet study, which found that late trauma-center tourniquet use was associated with worsened physiology, higher transfusion within the first hour of arrival, and higher mortality from hemorrhagic shock compared to pre-hospital tourniquet use [N5-F4]. In that study, delayed tourniquet use had 4.5-fold increased odds of death from hemorrhagic shock compared to early pre-hospital tourniquet use, and this association remained after controlling for year of admission, mechanism of injury, and shock upon arrival [N5-F4]. This is one of the clearest examples in the evidence base that tourniquet use can be protective, especially when applied early.

Other studies and meta-analyses show a more mixed picture. A meta-analysis of pre-hospital tourniquet studies reported that PH-TQ use did not appear to significantly influence mortality; the adjusted odds ratio was 0.47 (95% CI 0.19–1.16), and the evidence was downgraded to very low certainty [N1-F1]. Another meta-analysis of limb hemorrhage found a non-statistically significant reduction in mortality risk with tourniquet application (4.02% vs. 6.43%, RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46–1.07), with no significant reduction in mortality or blood product use [N1-F3]. A civilian prehospital tourniquet review similarly noted that most studies were highly heterogeneous with low-quality evidence and that most reported increased survival in the tourniquet group, but few had relevant comparators, making it difficult to estimate survival benefit directly [N2-R1][N2-R2]. A study comparing civilian prehospital tourniquet use with non-tourniquet use reported mortality of 5.2% in the non-tourniquet group versus 3.9% in the tourniquet group, but the association was not statistically significant (odds ratio 1.36; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.65; p = 0.452) [N4-R4]. These results suggest that while tourniquet use is often associated with lower mortality, the effect is not consistently strong or statistically robust.

## How do retrospective cohort studies compare mortality outcomes between pre-hospital tourniquet application and other types of tourniquet use in trauma patients?

Retrospective cohort studies and related observational evidence show that the relationship between tourniquet use and mortality in trauma patients is **mixed and not uniformly supportive of a strong benefit**, especially when comparing different tourniquet use categories or settings. The most direct comparisons in the evidence base suggest that **early pre-hospital tourniquet use is associated with better outcomes than delayed tourniquet use or no tourniquet use**, but the overall evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and often weak in certainty [N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-R1][N1-F3].

### 1) What types of studies are being compared?

The evidence base includes a mix of **retrospective cohort studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses**. These studies often compare:

- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** versus **no tourniquet use**,  
- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** versus **delayed trauma-center tourniquet use**,  
- **Tourniquet use** versus **other bleeding control measures**,  
- **Tourniquet use** versus **direct pressure or hemostatic dressings** [N1-F1][N1-F3][N2-R1][N5-F4].

A major limitation is that many studies are observational, which makes direct causal inference difficult [N1-F1]. The most relevant meta-analyses explicitly note that the evidence is observational and that certainty was downgraded to **very low** for mortality outcomes [N1-F1]. The civilian prehospital tourniquet review similarly concludes that the evidence is low quality and highly heterogeneous, with most studies reporting increased survival in the tourniquet group but few having relevant comparators [N2-R1][N2-R2].

### 2) What does the evidence say about mortality outcomes?

#### A) Overall mortality estimates
Across the evidence, mortality estimates are generally low, but the confidence intervals are wide, and the results are often **not statistically significant**.

- A meta-analysis of pre-hospital tourniquet studies reported an **adjusted odds ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.19–1.16)** for mortality, suggesting a possible benefit but not a clear or consistent one [N1-F1].
- A meta-analysis of limb hemorrhage found a **non-statistically significant reduction in mortality risk** with tourniquet application: **4.02% vs. 6.43%**, RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.46–1.07) [N1-F3].
- A civilian prehospital tourniquet review reported that most studies were highly heterogeneous with low-quality evidence, and most studies reported increased survival in the tourniquet group, but few had relevant comparators, making survival benefit difficult to estimate directly [N2-R1][N2-R2].
- A study comparing civilian prehospital tourniquet use with non-tourniquet use reported **mortality of 5.2% in the non-tourniquet group** versus **3.9% in the tourniquet group**, but the association was **not statistically significant** (odds ratio 1.36; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.65; p = 0.452) [N4-R4].

#### B) Direct comparison between pre-hospital tourniquet application and other tourniquet use
The clearest direct comparison in the evidence base is the **trauma-center tourniquet study**, which distinguishes **pre-hospital tourniquet use** from **delayed trauma-center tourniquet use** [N5-F4].

- In that study, **delayed tourniquet use** was associated with worse physiology, higher transfusion within the first hour of arrival, and **higher mortality from hemorrhagic shock** compared to **pre-hospital tourniquet use**.
- After controlling for year of admission, mechanism of injury, and shock upon arrival, **delayed tourniquet use had 4.5-fold increased odds of death** compared to **pre-hospital tourniquet use** [N5-F4].

This study is important because it shows that **the timing and setting of tourniquet application matter**: earlier pre-hospital use appears to be associated with better outcomes than delayed hospital-based use [N5-F4].

### 3) Do outcomes differ by trauma mechanism or injury severity?

Yes, the evidence suggests that outcomes can differ by **setting and injury context**.

- The trauma-center tourniquet study found that **70% of patients had blunt mechanism of injury**, and it controlled for **mechanism of injury**, **shock upon arrival**, and **year of admission** [N5-F4].
- The broader evidence base is also heterogeneous, with studies varying by trauma mechanism, injury severity, and setting [N2-R1][N2-R2][N1-F1].
- This means that mortality may depend on the **type of injury** and the **patient’s condition at presentation**, not just whether a tourniquet was used.

### 4) How do studies classify different tourniquet types?

Trauma literature often defines tourniquet use by **setting and timing** rather than by a strict device-type distinction [N3-R2][N5-F4].

- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** typically refers to tourniquet application by EMS, first responders, or lay responders at the scene or during transport [N3-R2].
- **Other tourniquet use** can be interpreted more broadly, including **trauma-center tourniquet use** or **other contemporaneous bleeding control measures** [N5-F4][N1-F3].

This classification is important because it affects outcome interpretation: a study comparing **pre-hospital tourniquet use** with **delayed hospital tourniquet use** may show a benefit of early application, whereas a study comparing **tourniquet use** with **no tourniquet use** may show a more modest or inconsistent effect [N5-F4][N1-F1].

### 5) What are the methodologic limitations?

The methodologic quality of the available evidence is a major concern. Retrospective cohort studies and observational meta-analyses are especially vulnerable to:

- **Confounding**: Many studies are observational, so factors such as injury severity, mechanism, physiology, and indication status may distort the observed association [N1-F1][N2-R1].
- **Indication bias**: Studies often separate patients by indication status, which can reflect selection rather than a true treatment effect [N5-F4][N2-R1].
- **Selection bias**: Retrospective cohort designs may capture only patients who received tourniquets or who had identifiable outcomes, which can bias the sample [N1-F1][N2-R2].
- **Heterogeneity**: The evidence base is highly heterogeneous, with studies differing in population, setting, injury severity, and outcome ascertainment [N2-R1][N1-F1].
- **Outcome measurement and adjustment**: Some studies report mortality and adjust for key covariates, which is a strength, but many studies also report less robust outcomes such as transfusion requirements or amputation, with weaker evidence [N1-F1][N1-F3][N4-R4].

### 6) What is the overall conclusion?

The best-supported conclusion from the evidence is that **retrospective cohort studies and observational reviews do not show a clear, consistent mortality benefit of pre-hospital tourniquet application over no tourniquet use** [N1-F1][N2-R1][N1-F3].

- The strongest direct comparison is the trauma-center tourniquet study, which found that **delayed tourniquet use was associated with worse outcomes** than **pre-hospital tourniquet use** [N5-F4].
- Other studies report lower mortality in the tourniquet group, but the results are often **not statistically significant**, **heterogeneous**, or based on **low-certainty evidence** [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-R4].
- Outcomes also appear to differ by **setting and injury context**, with worse outcomes in delayed hospital-based use and more favorable outcomes in earlier pre-hospital application [N5-F4].
- Because the evidence is observational, the results should be interpreted cautiously, and the observed associations may reflect selection, indication, or other biases rather than a robust causal effect [N1-F1][N2-R1].

### 7) Bottom line

In summary, retrospective cohort studies and related observational evidence suggest that **pre-hospital tourniquet application is associated with better outcomes than delayed or no tourniquet use in some settings**, especially when hemorrhage control is delayed until the trauma center [N5-F4]. However, the overall evidence is **mixed, heterogeneous, and limited in certainty**, so the benefit is not uniformly strong or consistent [N1-F1][N2-R1][N1-F3]. The best-supported interpretation is that **early, pre-hospital tourniquet use may be more protective than later tourniquet use or no tourniquet use**, but this remains an observational inference with important methodologic caveats [N5-F4][N1-F1].

## How do retrospective cohort studies compare mortality outcomes between pre-hospital tourniquet application and other types of tourniquet use in trauma patients?

Retrospective cohort studies and related observational evidence show that the relationship between tourniquet use and mortality in trauma patients is **mixed and not uniformly supportive of a strong benefit**, especially when comparing different tourniquet use categories or settings. The most direct comparisons in the evidence base suggest that **early pre-hospital tourniquet use is associated with better outcomes than delayed tourniquet use or no tourniquet use**, but the overall evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and often weak in certainty [N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-R1][N1-F3].

### 1) What types of studies are being compared?

The evidence base includes a mix of **retrospective cohort studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses**. These studies often compare:

- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** versus **no tourniquet use**,  
- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** versus **delayed trauma-center tourniquet use**,  
- **Tourniquet use** versus **other bleeding control measures**,  
- **Tourniquet use** versus **direct pressure or hemostatic dressings** [N1-F1][N1-F3][N2-R1][N5-F4].

A major limitation is that many studies are observational, which makes direct causal inference difficult [N1-F1]. The most relevant meta-analyses explicitly note that the evidence is observational and that certainty was downgraded to **very low** for mortality outcomes [N1-F1]. The civilian prehospital tourniquet review similarly concludes that the evidence is low quality and highly heterogeneous, with most studies reporting increased survival in the tourniquet group but few having relevant comparators [N2-R1][N2-R2].

### 2) What does the evidence say about mortality outcomes?

#### A) Overall mortality estimates
Across the evidence, mortality estimates are generally low, but the confidence intervals are wide, and the results are often **not statistically significant**.

- A meta-analysis of pre-hospital tourniquet studies reported an **adjusted odds ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.19–1.16)** for mortality, suggesting a possible benefit but not a clear or consistent one [N1-F1].
- A meta-analysis of limb hemorrhage found a **non-statistically significant reduction in mortality risk** with tourniquet application: **4.02% vs. 6.43%**, RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.46–1.07) [N1-F3].
- A civilian prehospital tourniquet review reported that most studies were highly heterogeneous with low-quality evidence, and most studies reported increased survival in the tourniquet group, but few had relevant comparators, making survival benefit difficult to estimate directly [N2-R1][N2-R2].

#### B) Direct comparison between pre-hospital tourniquet application and other tourniquet use
The clearest direct comparison in the evidence base is the **trauma-center tourniquet study**, which distinguishes **pre-hospital tourniquet use** from **delayed trauma-center tourniquet use** [N5-F4].

- In that study, **delayed tourniquet use** was associated with worse physiology, higher transfusion within the first hour of arrival, and **higher mortality from hemorrhagic shock** compared to **pre-hospital tourniquet use**.
- After controlling for year of admission, mechanism of injury, and shock upon arrival, **delayed tourniquet use had 4.5-fold increased odds of death** compared to **pre-hospital tourniquet use** [N5-F4].

This study is important because it shows that **the timing and setting of tourniquet application matter**: earlier pre-hospital use appears to be associated with better outcomes than delayed hospital-based use [N5-F4].

### 3) Do outcomes differ by trauma mechanism or injury severity?

Yes, the evidence suggests that outcomes can differ by **setting and injury context**.

- The trauma-center tourniquet study found that **70% of patients had blunt mechanism of injury**, and it controlled for **mechanism of injury**, **shock upon arrival**, and **year of admission** [N5-F4].
- The broader evidence base is also heterogeneous, with studies varying by trauma mechanism, injury severity, and setting [N2-R1][N2-R2][N1-F1].
- This means that mortality may depend on the **type of injury** and the **patient’s condition at presentation**, not just whether a tourniquet was used.

### 4) How do studies classify different tourniquet types?

Trauma literature often defines tourniquet use by **setting and timing** rather than by a strict device-type distinction [N3-R2][N5-F4].

- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** typically refers to tourniquet application by EMS, first responders, or lay responders at the scene or during transport [N3-R2].
- **Other tourniquet use** can be interpreted more broadly, including **trauma-center tourniquet use** or **other contemporaneous bleeding control measures** [N5-F4][N1-F3].
- In some studies, “other” tourniquet use is contrasted with direct pressure, hemostatic dressings, or other bleeding control techniques [N1-F3].

This classification is important because it affects outcome interpretation: a study comparing **pre-hospital tourniquet use** with **delayed hospital tourniquet use** may show a benefit of early application, whereas a study comparing **tourniquet use** with **no tourniquet use** may show a more modest or inconsistent effect [N5-F4][N1-F1].

### 5) What are the methodologic limitations?

- **Confounding**: Many studies are observational, so factors such as injury severity, mechanism, physiology, and indication status may distort the observed association [N1-F1][N2-R1].
- **Indication bias**: Studies often separate patients by indication status, which can reflect selection rather than a true treatment effect [N5-F4][N2-R1].
- **Selection bias**: Retrospective cohort designs may capture only patients who received tourniquets or who had identifiable outcomes, which can bias the sample [N1-F1][N2-R2].
- **Heterogeneity**: The evidence base is highly heterogeneous, with studies differing in population, setting, injury severity, and outcome ascertainment [N2-R1][N1-F1].
- **Outcome measurement and adjustment**: Some studies report mortality and adjust for key covariates, which is a strength, but many studies also report less robust outcomes such as transfusion requirements or amputation, with weaker evidence [N1-F1][N1-F3][N4-R4].

### 6) What is the overall conclusion?

The best-supported conclusion from the evidence is that **retrospective cohort studies and observational reviews do not show a clear, consistent mortality benefit of pre-hospital tourniquet application over no tourniquet use** [N1-F1][N2-R1][N1-F3].

- The strongest direct comparison is the trauma-center tourniquet study, which found that **delayed tourniquet use was associated with worse outcomes** than **pre-hospital tourniquet use** [N5-F4].

- Outcomes also appear to differ by **setting and injury context**, with worse outcomes in delayed hospital-based use and more favorable outcomes in earlier pre-hospital application [N5-F4].
- Because the evidence is observational, the results should be interpreted cautiously, and the observed associations may reflect selection, indication, or other biases rather than a robust causal effect [N1-F1][N2-R1].

In summary, retrospective cohort studies and related observational evidence suggest that **pre-hospital tourniquet application is associated with better outcomes than delayed or no tourniquet use in some settings**, especially when hemorrhage control is delayed until the trauma center [N5-F4]. However, the overall evidence is **mixed, heterogeneous, and limited in certainty**, so the benefit is not uniformly strong or consistent [N1-F1][N2-R1][N1-F3]. The best-supported interpretation is that **early, pre-hospital tourniquet use may be more protective than later tourniquet use or no tourniquet use**, but this remains an observational inference with important methodologic caveats [N5-F4][N1-F1].

## How do retrospective cohort studies compare mortality outcomes between pre-hospital tourniquet application and other types of tourniquet use in trauma patients?

Retrospective cohort studies and related observational evidence show that the relationship between tourniquet use and mortality in trauma patients is **mixed and not uniformly supportive of a strong benefit**, especially when comparing different tourniquet use categories or settings. The most direct comparisons in the evidence base suggest that **early pre-hospital tourniquet use is associated with better outcomes than delayed tourniquet use or no tourniquet use**, but the overall evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and often weak in certainty [N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-R1][N1-F3].

### 1) What types of studies are being compared?

The evidence base includes a mix of **retrospective cohort studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses**. These studies often compare:

- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** versus **no tourniquet use**,  
- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** versus **delayed trauma-center tourniquet use**,  
- **Tourniquet use** versus **other bleeding control measures**,  
- **Tourniquet use** versus **direct pressure or hemostatic dressings** [N1-F1][N1-F3][N2-R1][N5-F4].

A major limitation is that many studies are observational, which makes direct causal inference difficult [N1-F1]. The most relevant meta-analyses explicitly note that the evidence is observational and that certainty was downgraded to **very low** for mortality outcomes [N1-F1]. The civilian prehospital tourniquet review similarly concludes that the evidence is low quality and highly heterogeneous, with most studies reporting increased survival in the tourniquet group but few having relevant comparators [N2-R1][N2-R2].

### 2) What does the evidence say about mortality outcomes?

#### A) Overall mortality estimates
Across the evidence, mortality estimates are generally low, but the confidence intervals are wide, and the results are often **not statistically significant**.

- A meta-analysis of pre-hospital tourniquet studies reported an **adjusted odds ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.19–1.16)** for mortality, suggesting a possible benefit but not a clear or consistent one [N1-F1].
- A meta-analysis of limb hemorrhage found a **non-statistically significant reduction in mortality risk** with tourniquet application: **4.02% vs. 6.43%**, RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.46–1.07) [N1-F3].
- A civilian prehospital tourniquet review reported that most studies were highly heterogeneous with low-quality evidence, and most studies reported increased survival in the tourniquet group, but few had relevant comparators, making survival benefit difficult to estimate directly [N2-R1][N2-R2].
- A study comparing civilian prehospital tourniquet use with non-tourniquet use reported **mortality of 5.2% in the non-tourniquet group** versus **3.9% in the tourniquet group**, but the association was **not statistically significant** (odds ratio 1.36; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.65; p = 0.452) [N4-R4].

#### B) Direct comparison between pre-hospital tourniquet application and other tourniquet use
The clearest direct comparison in the evidence base is the **trauma-center tourniquet study**, which distinguishes **pre-hospital tourniquet use** from **delayed trauma-center tourniquet use** [N5-F4].

- In that study, **delayed tourniquet use** was associated with worse physiology, higher transfusion within the first hour of arrival, and **higher mortality from hemorrhagic shock** compared to **pre-hospital tourniquet use**.
- After controlling for year of admission, mechanism of injury, and shock upon arrival, **delayed tourniquet use had 4.5-fold increased odds of death** compared to **pre-hospital tourniquet use** [N5-F4].

This study is important because it shows that **the timing and setting of tourniquet application matter**: earlier pre-hospital use appears to be associated with better outcomes than delayed hospital-based use [N5-F4].

### 3) Do outcomes differ by trauma mechanism or injury severity?

Yes, the evidence suggests that outcomes can differ by **setting and injury context**.

- The trauma-center tourniquet study found that **70% of patients had blunt mechanism of injury**, and it controlled for **mechanism of injury**, **shock upon arrival**, and **year of admission** [N5-F4].
- The broader evidence base is also heterogeneous, with studies varying by trauma mechanism, injury severity, and setting [N2-R1][N2-R2][N1-F1].
- This means that mortality may depend on the **type of injury** and the **patient’s condition at presentation**, not just whether a tourniquet was used.

### 4) How do studies classify different tourniquet types?

Trauma literature often defines tourniquet use by **setting and timing** rather than by a strict device-type distinction [N3-R2][N5-F4].

- **Pre-hospital tourniquet use** typically refers to tourniquet application by EMS, first responders, or lay responders at the scene or during transport [N3-R2].
- **Other tourniquet use** can be interpreted more broadly, including **trauma-center tourniquet use** or **other contemporaneous bleeding control measures** [N5-F4][N1-F3].
